paragraphs.heading: The circular argument
paragraphs.edited: See, the problem is that often we get stuck in this loop where we ask the question, how do I know that the Bible is true? Well, then we say, that's because the Bible says so. Well, how do I know that the Bible says so? Well, because I know the Bible is true. And we just keep going in a circle, over and over and over again, and we never actually have anything exterior that helps us understand whether or not the Bible is actually true. We throw in there a little bit of, well, it's the inspired — I can't write — the inspired word of God. And therefore it must be true, and it must be because the Bible says so, because it's the inspired word of God, because we know it's true, and we go on and on that way.

paragraphs.heading: Autographs and manuscripts
paragraphs.edited: Well, what's fascinating about that is that we have what's called an autograph and a manuscript. An autograph is an original copy. It's as if I actually gave my autograph, my signature. It's original to me. I wrote it, and only I can write it. That's essentially what we're talking about when we say an autograph. When we talk about texts from antiquity — the ancient texts, those biblical times and earlier and all around that era — we have no autographs. We have nothing originally written by anybody in their physical hand. But what we do have is manuscripts, copies. Sometimes they are copies of a copy of a copy; that is entirely possible.

paragraphs.heading: Documents that prove something
paragraphs.edited: So to start this process, we ask students in the introduction activity to look up a legal document that proves their existence. Think about it: you have a birth certificate, you have a driver's license, you can't get on an airplane without a driver's license or a passport. You're often asked for your Social Security card any time your identity is checked for a job or that kind of thing, right? So you have to have some kind of proof of your existence, proof that you are who you say you are. We have these legally binding documents that are proof of something. So we want students to start to see that there are documents out there even today that have this kind of power.
